rows: [Margin, p. 323: Nodus VII. Quomodo Deus propter suam bonitatem mundum condiderit?]
[Margin, p. 323: Knot VII. How God on account of His goodness [bonitatem] founded [condiderit] the world?]

Asphal. Nescio quomodo fiat ut cum eripueris nos ex unis angustiis, in alias statim subeamus, quasi de Scylla in Charybdim eiecti. Ecce enim exposuisti quomodo Deus a creatis bonis non alliciatur. Sed nova oritur quaestio quo scilicet motivo mundum nobis condiderit? Cum enim bonum respectivum sit, ad eum dumtaxat bonum est qui pellici potest hoc bono ad actionem. Deus vero neque a totius mundi bonitate pellici ad actionem potest, quare neque bonus illi erit. Si vero non sit ei bonus, ipse vero propter bonitatem operatur, propter mundum operari non potest; Neque reponi potest propter suam bonitatem mundum creare, cum creatio mundi ad suam bonitatem nihil conducat.

Asphal. I know not how it comes about that, when you have snatched us out of one strait [ex unis angustiis], we straightway go under into others, as if cast out from Scylla into Charybdis. For see, you have expounded how God is not allured [alliciatur] by created goods. But a new question arises: by what motive [motivo], namely, He founded the world for us? For since good is relative [respectivum], it is good only to him who can be enticed [pellici] by this good to action. But God can be enticed to action not even [neque] by the goodness of the whole world; wherefore neither will it [the world] be good to Him. But if it be not good to Him, and He Himself works on account of goodness, He cannot work on account of the world; nor can it be replied [reponi] that He creates the world on account of His goodness, since the creation of the world contributes nothing to His goodness.

Ereu. Immo vero propter suam bonitatem, & facit, & facere potest. Nonne vides enim etiam nos misereri pauperis, a quo neque utilitatem, neque honorem expectare possumus, non alia de causa quam quia conforme est naturae rationali? Cogita itaque tecum hominem sollicitum ut animam suam iis actibus exerceat, qui secundum naturam sunt: & non vides ex eo solo quod ipse quaerat animam secundum rationem constitutam habere, sequi ut multam beneficentiam proximis exhibeat? Si enim habeat voluntatem secundum rationem directam, quoties ratio dicet benefaciendum esse, toties volet benefacere, ex voluntate vero sequitur effectus; vides itaque quomodo signate ex eo quod intrinsecum sibi bonum appetat, exterior operatio sequatur.

Ereu. Nay rather, on account of His goodness He both does [it] and can do [it]. For do you not see that we too pity a poor man, from whom we can expect neither utility [utilitatem] nor honour, for no other cause than because it is conformable to rational nature? Think, therefore, with yourself of a man solicitous that he may exercise his soul in those acts which are according to nature: and do you not see that from this alone, that he himself seeks to have [his] soul constituted according to reason, it follows that he shows much beneficence to [his] neighbours [proximis]? For if he have a will directed according to reason, as often as reason shall say that good is to be done [benefaciendum esse], so often will he will to do good; and from the will follows the effect; you see therefore how, expressly [signate], from this, that he desires the good intrinsic to himself, the exterior operation follows.

Hoc Deo iuxta applica; & quoniam Deus diligit se ex necessitate, sequitur velle habere, voluntatem ea agendi quae Deo digna sunt. Inter quae, cum primum sit mundum condere, voluntatem habebit condendi mundum, non propter bonitatem mundi conditi, sed propter bonitatem quae est in voluntate condendi mundi. Rectam enim esse voluntatem etiam Deo bonum est.

Apply this likewise [iuxta] to God; and since God loves [diligit] Himself of necessity, it follows [that He] wills to have a will of doing those things which are worthy of God. Among which, since the first is to found the world, He will have a will of founding the world, not on account of the goodness of the world founded, but on account of the goodness which is in the will of founding the world. For that the will be right [rectam] is good even to God.

Asphal. Verum cum nihil boni sit, Deo condere mundum, quomodo non recta erit ei voluntas, nisi de condendo mundo sit? Voluntas enim recta est, quia de bono est; si itaque non propterea est de bono, quia est de conditione mundi, neque propterea recta erit quia de eo, vel non recta si non de eo.

Asphal. But since it is nothing of good to God to found the world, how will the will not be right for Him, unless it be about founding the world? For a will is right because it is about good; if therefore it is not about good for this reason, that it is about the founding [conditione] of the world, neither will it be right for this reason, that [it is] about it, or not right if not about it.

Ereu. Non vides rationi duo bonorum genera esse, alterum quod vocant honestum, alterum utile. Hoc autem non habere boni rationem per se, sed ex priori tanquam quod honesti effecti unum sit, nosti enim denominationem Analogicam effectui posse convenire aeque atque causae; sicut enim cibum vel medicinam sanam dicimus, quod causet sanitatem, sic urinam vel alia excrementa ex eo quod a sanitate proficiscuntur, sana appellamus, perfectionem autem bonitatem dicimus.

Ereu. You do not see [that] to reason there are two kinds of goods, the one which they call the honest [honestum], the other the useful [utile]. And that this [latter] does not have the notion [rationem] of good through itself, but from the prior, as being one [thing] of the honest [good] effected [honesti effecti unum]; for you know that an Analogical denomination can belong to the effect equally as to the cause; for just as we call food or medicine healthy [sanam], because it causes health, so urine or other excrements, from this, that they proceed from health, we call healthy; but perfection we call goodness.

Quod ergo imperfecto est causa perfectionis, merito bonum illi, hoc est, utile appellamus, sed respectu perfecti cessat bonum in hac appellatione. Quoniam vero ex perfectione sequitur aliquid, verbi gratia, facere simile sibi, hoc etiam dicitur bonum tanquam boni effectus.

What therefore is to the imperfect a cause of perfection, we deservedly call good to it, that is, useful; but in respect of the perfect, good ceases in this appellation. But since from perfection something follows, for example [verbi gratia], to make [something] like to itself, this too is called good, as an effect of good.

Quandoquidem itaque Deus undique perfectus est, non est quaerendum in illo bonum priori modo: quod enim est, non indiget causa ut fiat. Sed hoc posteriori modo potest reperiri, respectu ipsius quod appellationem boni Analogice subire potest: Sed non tale ut alliciat voluntatem: hoc enim bono per se tantum competit. Sed tale ut per aliud voluntas ad illud alliciatur. Et sic ex dilectione voluntatis conformis suae naturae derivatur Deus ad condendum terrarum orbem.

Since therefore God is on every side perfect, good is not to be sought in Him in the former mode: for what is, does not need a cause that it may come to be. But it can be found in this latter mode, in respect of that itself which can undergo the appellation of good Analogically: but not such as to allure the will: for this belongs [competit] only to good through itself [per se]. But such that through another the will is allured to it. And thus from the love [dilectione] of a will conformable to His own nature God is drawn down [derivatur] to founding the orb of the lands [terrarum orbem].
Andab. Ais itaque non rectam futuram Dei voluntatem, nisi condendi universi auctrix foret.
Andab. You say therefore that the will of God would not be right, unless it were the authoress [auctrix] of founding the universe.
Ereu. Dixi.
Ereu. I have said [so] [Dixi].

Andab. At Deo naturale est non deficere a rectitudine voluntatis, & oppositum inter ea quae maxime potentiam fugiunt, reponendum. Non pote itaque Deus mundum non condere: neque libere, sed naturaliter hoc facit. Quod, nisi fallor, Ereuni, Philosophum & Peripateticum magis sapit, quam Christianum. Vide itaque ne aliquo impingas.

Andab. But to God it is natural not to fall short [deficere] from the rectitude of will, and the opposite [is] to be placed back [reponendum] among those things which most of all flee power [potentiam fugiunt]. God therefore cannot [pote] not found the world: nor does He do this freely [libere], but naturally [naturaliter]. Which, unless I am mistaken, Ereunius, savours [sapit] more of the Philosopher and the Peripatetic than of the Christian. See therefore lest you strike [impingas] somewhere.

terms: moral goodness; ontological perfection; the good as object of appetite.
White moves between good as perfection (bonitas = perfectio) and good as what allures the will; the Knot turns on which sense applies to God’s motive.
Asphalius’ premise: a good is only good to an agent who can be moved by it; hence the world cannot be ‘good to’ God.
moving reason, end that moves the will; scholastic ‘ratio movens’.
Scholastic term for the final cause as it moves an agent; cf. causalitas finalis in Knot vi.
Kept distinct; both name the final cause’s ‘drawing’ of the will, which White denies created goods exercise on God.
the morally noble, good for its own sake / the expedient, good for something else.
Ciceronian-Stoic division (De officiis) adopted by the scholastics (bonum honestum, utile, delectabile); White omits the delectabile.
Aristotle’s ‘healthy’ example (Metaph. Γ 2, 1003a34 ff.): food, medicine and urine are called healthy by reference to health; standard scholastic illustration of analogy of attribution.
Cf. signatum (D3-N04); here adverbial: the exterior work follows precisely from the inner desire.
alongside; in the same way (adverbial iuxta = pariter).
Anselmian ‘rectitudo voluntatis’; White makes God’s will right by conforming to His nature, which leads Andabata to infer necessity.
Ambiguous genitive in ‘dilectione voluntatis’: the will’s love, or love of a will conformable to God’s nature.
Metaphor of a stream diverted; God’s will ‘flows down’ to creation.
Classical idiom for the inhabited world; here = mundus.
Grammatical gender of voluntas; kept literally.
Things that ‘flee power’ are those not subject to (divine) power, i.e. contradictions; Andabata places God’s failing in rectitude among them.
by election vs. by necessity of nature.

The scholastic opposition of free (voluntary, contingent) and natural (necessary) agency; the charge that creation by necessity is Aristotelian (eternal necessary emanation) rather than Christian — leads into Knot viii ‘Deum libere mundum condidisse’.
Scholastic antonomasia for Aristotle; paired with Peripateticum.
Nautical image continuing Asphalius’ Scylla/Charybdis: beware of running onto a rock (heresy).
proverb: incidit in Scyllam qui vult vitare Charybdim.
Homer, Od. XII; proverbial escape from one danger into another.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot vii (complete). PDF pp. 334–337 = printed pp. 323–326, from Asphalius’ ‘Nescio quomodo fiat ut cum eripueris’ (p. 323, margin ‘Nodus VII. Quomodo Deus propter suam bonitatem mundum condiderit?’) to Andabata’s ‘Vide itaque ne aliquo impingas.’ (p. 326). Knot VIII (‘Deum liberum mundum condidisse’ in the margin; ‘Deum libere mundum condidisse’ in the table) begins on p. 326 (PDF 337) with Ereunius’ ‘Quod ad Theologiam & fidem spectat’. Offset +11 holds. Signatures: Ss ij (p. 323), Ss iij (p. 325).

Uncertain readings and constructions: (1) p. 325 ‘tanquam quod honesti effecti unum sit’ — clearly printed; ‘effecti’ taken as gen. sing. of the noun effectum, i.e. the useful is ‘one [thing] of the honest [good] effected’ (an effect of the honest); an emendation ‘honesti effectum’ would give the same sense. (2) p. 325 ‘Non vides … utile.’ is printed with a full stop, not a question mark; translated as a statement (‘You do not see …’), though a question is likely meant. (3) p. 326 ‘Non pote itaque’ — confirmed at 300 dpi; archaic pote = potest. (4) p. 326 ‘ex dilectione voluntatis conformis suae naturae’ — genitive ambiguous (the will’s love vs. love of a will); rendered ‘the love of a will’ to keep both open. (5) p. 324 ‘sequitur velle habere, voluntatem’ — comma as printed; voluntatem taken as object of habere. Spelling ‘expectare’ kept. No illegible readings.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images (zoomed at 300 dpi on pp. 324 and 326) and against the English. The check produced 3 corrections: (i) p. 324 ‘Deus vero neque a totius mundi bonitate pellici … potest’ — first drafted as ‘neither by the goodness…’ as if correlative; corrected to ‘not even [neque]’, the second neque (‘quare neque’) being independent; (ii) p. 326 ‘ex dilectione voluntatis’ — first drafted ‘the love of the will’; changed to ‘of a will’ to keep the objective reading open (see note 4); (iii) p. 325 ‘Non vides rationi duo bonorum genera esse’ — first drafted as a question (‘Do you not see…?’); corrected to a statement to follow the printed full stop (see note 2).

Conventions: as in previous units (see glossary.md). Ereunius’ two longer speeches are split at sense-breaks (continuation rows carry no speaker head). condere = found; bonitas = goodness; ratio (boni) = notion [rationem].
